events.excerpt: arXiv:2602.02412v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has made the generation of synthetic images widely accessible, increasing concerns related to misinformation, digital forgery, and content authenticity on large-scale online platforms. This paper proposes a registry-based framework for verifying AI-generated images through a registry-based provenance mechanism. Each AI-generated image is assigned a digital fingerprint that preserves similarity using perceptual hashing and is registered at creation time by participating generation platforms. The Merkle Patricia Trie, provides prefix-based organization and cryptographic integrity of the registry structure, while Burkhard-Keller tree enable similarity search based on Hamming distance. Verification is performed when images are re-uploaded to digital platforms such as social media services, enabling identification of previously registered AI-generated images even after benign transformations or partial modifications. The proposed system does not aim to universally detect all synthetic images, but instead focuses on verifying the provenance of AI-generated content that has been registered at creation time. By design, this approach complements existing watermarking and learning-based detection methods, providing a platform-agnostic, tamper-evident mechanism for scalable content provenance and verification at the point of large scale online distribution.
events.title: Provenance Verification of AI-Generated Images via a Perceptual Hash Registry Using Merkle Patricia Trie and BK-Tree

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local-first security tools let organizations analyze code without sending it to third-party services, but the small language models they can run locally are weaker than hosted ones and are hard to improve without breaching the privacy guarantee that motivates them. We report its measured v0.3.0 baseline on a synthetic, ground-truth benchmark: combining Semgrep with an interprocedural call-graph scanner yields precision 0.843 and recall 0.915 (Semgrep alone: 0.818 and 0.766). The advisory layer is the weak point: 57% of explanations met an evidence-grounding check, against 95% for a different 8B model under identical prompts. events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11438v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.
events.title: When Coding Agents Get Arms: Safety Risks Across the Digital-Physical Boundary

events.excerpt: The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices. Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash. "Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins. "About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs." Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare. Its latest report, " An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent ," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register , have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use. At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources

It has no hardfork and no activation timestamp: every change is applied through a signed superchain-ops execution on L1. It contains the following changes: ETHLockbox as custody and pause identifier — every chain gets an ETHLockbox that cannot be disabled, and it becomes the only identifier for a chain-specific pause. events.excerpt: CometBFT v0.38.25 can’t read an ML-DSA public key. Its PubKeyFromProto knows Ed25519 and secp256k1, and its MaxSignatureSize is 64 bytes, while an ML-DSA-65 signature is 3,309. The Quarterly says post-quantum consensus keys shipped with SDK v0.55 and CometBFT v0.40, and that the Hub moves to v30 once ibc-go carries v0.55. Before any chain lets its validators use those keys, I wanted to know what breaks on the other side of its IBC connections, so I read the rotation code and the light clients. The SDK docs already say every counterparty must upgrade before the first validator rotates. This is what I’d add to that. v0.38.26 is enough for a Go counterparty The docs ask counterparties for CometBFT v0.40. On the 0.38 line there’s a smaller step. v0.38.26 (13 August, PR 6028 ) backports only ML-DSA decoding and verification, “for the purposes of verification of IBC connections with counterparty chains that are on v0.40”, and raises MaxSignatureSize to 3,309. It doesn’t let the chain itself use the key. So a chain on SDK v0.53 doesn’t need the v0.55 migration for its own clients of an ML-DSA chain, a patch release on the line it’s on covers it.
